newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Bolshoi boss sees threat of closure, disaster.
newsitem.headline: Bolshoi boss sees threat of closure, disaster.

text.p: Moscow's Bolshoi Theatre, an icon of the arts world tarnished by money troubles since the collapse of communism, is living from hand to mouth and could have to close for lack of funds, its artistic director warned on Monday.

"Where are we going to get money? If we don't, the question of closure will come up again. We just won't be able to open (next season)," Vladimir Vasilyev told a news conference following Sunday's final performance of the 1996-97 season.
"I can't rule out that part of the balcony might just collapse," the former leading man of the Bolshoi ballet added.

Vasilyev's warnings are not new. The hard-pressed Russian government and Moscow city council have, with the help of private sponsors, managed to keep the theatre, a magnet for tourists, open for daily performances of opera and ballet.

President Boris Yeltsin and the mayor of Moscow have pledged that an ambitious makeover of the exquisite 19th century theatre, including the building of a new 1,000-seat auditorium, will be completed, though quite when is not altogether clear.

But Vasilyev's complaints about the level of funding reinforced his guarded outlook on his chances of restoring the Bolshoi's artistic reputation, badly damaged by the departures of star performers to the West and accusations that his predecessor, who was sacked in 1995, had run out of ideas.
"We just don't have the money for new productions," he said.
Some new productions -- mostly from a repertoire comprised largely of Russian classics by the likes of Tchaikovsky and Rimsky-Korsakov -- had not been "adequate", he acknowledged.

But improvements took time and the 221-year-old company could not afford to ditch productions, some of which have been running with few changes since the early days of the autocratic 30-year reign of Vasilyev's predecessor, Yuri Grigorovich.
Vasilyev said government funding of about $12 million a year was enough only to cover the Bolshoi's wage bill.

Staging an opera cost between $500,000 and $1 million, he said. But ticket sales for the whole of last year brought in only about $2 million, leaving the Bolshoi dependent on scarce private sponsorship as it tries to rejuvenate its repertoire.
Stung by some recents hiccups on foreign tours, Vasilyev said the ballet company would limit its travels for now but hoped to make a full-scale American tour in 1999.

Foreign tours ought to be a money-spinner for the Bolshoi, one of the world's most recognisable names in classical music. Vasilyev blamed poor organisation for the ballet playing to empty houses in the gambling resort of Las Vegas.

Vasilyev also hopes to attract more big-name foreign stars to Moscow. Tickets cost as little as a couple of dollars for domestic performances -- the minimum in the West is about 10 times that -- but foreign stars push prices up.

British actor-director Peter Ustinov is due to present a new production of Prokofiev's opera "Love for Three Oranges" in November and the Spanish diva Montserrat Caballe will sing during Moscow's 850th anniversary celebrations in September.
